extracted.intended_audience: scientists, experimentalists, and advanced students of scientific method / philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for designing, conducting, interpreting, and defending experimental scientific work — including how to weigh observations, handle discrepancies (residual phenomena), and the personal/ intellectual qualities required of experimental investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated determinations by distinct methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of repeated determinations by distinct methods in disabusing our minds of the reliance which we are apt to place in results which show a certain degree of coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, obtain independent determinations of the same quantity by different experimental approaches; discrepant but coincident-looking results can mislead. Example: differing determinations of the Earth's mean density (Baily vs Airy) show the need for repeated, varied measurements to reveal method-dependent bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting and rejecting earlier results when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: When increased care in later observations produces systematically different estimates, it may be requisite to reject earlier results rather than treat all determinations as of equal weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mechanically average all historical measurements; consider probable and mean errors, and give greater credence to recent, more careful series (illustrated by Baily's and Airy's higher, later estimates of Earth's density).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-method consistency for physical constants
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine important constants by a variety of almost entirely distinct modes and compare results; consistency across methods increases confidence in the accepted value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the mechanical equivalent of heat was obtained by friction experiments, gas-measurements, steam-engine work, electrical heat, etc.; the mean of these methods (and closeness to Joule's best method) supports the chosen constant (e.g., ≈423·55 kg·m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and investigation of residual phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Outstanding discrepancies between theory and observation (residual phenomena) must be carefully examined; they may arise from (i) some known agent not previously suspected, or (ii) some new agent of unknown nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat residuals as important clues rather than nuisances. Classify whether they can be reconciled with known causes (e.g., electrical effects, meteoric swarms) or whether they indicate genuinely new phenomena (example: Encke's comet's period shortening prompted hypotheses such as resisting media or electrical/meteoric causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use residuals as avenues to discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Residual differences, when real, are the natural places to look for new discoveries; many major astronomical and physical discoveries were first noticed as systematic residuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain systematic comparison of observations with theoretical expectations (as introduced at well-conducted observatories); historic examples include nutation, aberration, planetary perturbations, and the discovery of Neptune from Uranus's residual deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful recording and continuing investigation of discrepancies
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is more requisite for the progress of science than the careful recording and investigation of discrepancies; gradual theoretical and measurement improvements will resolve whether an anomaly is error or new fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent, precise record-keeping of residuals and anomalies enables later theoretical advances (Newton's, Laplace's corrections). Treat small residuals cautiously but keep them under observation for patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize experiments by likely scientific yield
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate resources to experiments that will most advance understanding rather than to ceremonious or low-yield expeditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues funds spent on large observational expeditions (e.g., transits of Venus) might be better spent on experiments likely to yield critical constants or resolve residuals (e.g., renewed determinations of Earth's density, repeating pendulum experiments in different mines or mountains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind receptive to exceptional phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural philosopher must have a mind of impressionable character, affected by the slightest exceptional phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should cultivate sensitivity to oddities; noticing an exceptional datum is the first step toward associating it with other facts and forming hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associative and identifying powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimentalist's associating and identifying powers must be great; a strange fact should suggest whatever of like nature has previously come within experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong analogical thinking helps generate hypotheses that relate anomalous observations to known phenomena; this is distinct from mere accumulation of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active imagination and deductive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination must be active, bringing before the mind multitudes of relations in which unexplained facts may stand with respect to each other; sure and vigorous deductive powers are then required to infer consequences under each supposed condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent speculative hypotheses freely, but follow them with rigorous deductive tests and experimental checks (Faraday and Kepler exemplify imaginative hypothesis with rigorous testing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of certainty and candour in testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Above all there must be the love of certainty leading the investigator diligently and with perfect candour to compare his speculations with the test of fact and experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should openly acknowledge failures and negative results (Kepler's acknowledged errors; Faraday's candour about speculative shadows); truth requires frank testing and admission of mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of theorising (tolerance for many false guesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fertility of imagination and abundance of guesses are among the first requisites of discovery; erroneous guesses must be many times more numerous than those proved well founded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow whimsical or weak analogies as trial hypotheses — nothing is really absurd except what contradicts logic and experience — but ensure they are subjected to experiment and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of mere Baconian accumulation as sufficient method
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of research consisting of indiscriminately gathering facts (Baconian bookkeeping) is unlikely to yield great discoveries; facts alone do not by routine disclosure reveal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid believing that exhaustive collection and cataloguing of data will automatically produce laws; philosophical insight and selective, hypothesis-driven analysis are needed because possible arrangements of facts are practically infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the Newtonian method: deduction plus experimental verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Great hypotheses should be developed by deductive reasoning and then brought to the touchstone of fact by experimental verification (the Newtonian method is the model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a series of inductions rise to causes, then descend to derive detailed consequences; use mathematical deduction where appropriate (Principia and Opticks as exemplars). Combine theory and precise experiment to establish laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match research problems to intellectual strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Different branches require different mental qualities (e.g., Newton's high mathematical genius vs Faraday's qualitative experimental genius); investigators should seek problems suited to their minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize whether one's talents are more mathematical/deductive or qualitative/experimental and choose research domains accordingly; both types are essential to scientific progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience and persistent labour are necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Patience is one of the most requisite components of genius, but patient labour alone will not invariably lead to great discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained effort increases the chance that a latent 'germ' of genius will bear fruit, but material resources and training cannot create genius where the creative faculty is absent.
